fetched_contents.title: Who Should Use a Pump? | ADA
fetched_contents.text: Who Should Use a Pump? Insulin pumps have been used successfully across the age spectrum. Whether or not to use a pump is a personal decision. You can manage your diabetes equally well with pumps or multiple injections, so it comes down to your preference. Choosing one method over the other is not a lifelong commitment. Some people go on and off their pumps (but this should always be done with instructions from a person’s diabetes care team). Remember that a pump is just a tool—you can reach blood glucose goals with a pump or injections. But here are some things to consider… Pump safety is a commitment The one absolute requirement for using a pump is that you and/or your caregivers are ready and willing to do what it takes to use the pump safely. Most diabetes providers and insurance companies require that you check your blood glucose at least four times per day before you go on an insulin pump. Checking blood glucose is important because it will warn you if your pump stops working right, or your infusion set stops working. This can cause high blood glucose levels and cause you can go into diabetes ketoacidosis, which is very serious and dangerous. Checking blood glucose levels frequently will alert you to this possibility and will prevent the development of ketones. When do you need an insulin pump? A pump might be considered for 1. People who like the idea of a pump. If this is what you want, or you want for your child, and it can be used it safely, then it should be used. 2. Active people, who benefit from changes in basal rates or suspending the pump when exercising. 3. People who have frequent low blood glucose reactions. 4. Anyone who has delays in absorption of food from the stomach (gastroparesis). 5. Women planning pregnancy. 6. People who want to use the pump’s bolus calculator functions to determine insulin doses. Other factors to consider 1. The insulin pump doesn’t take away the need to check blood glucose and give insulin before meal. 2. There are technical aspects to using a pump—setting it up, putting it in, interacting with it—that are more complicated in some ways than using injections. 3. It only gives shorter-acting insulin. If it breaks or falls off, the person wearing it needs to be ready to give insulin by injection any time it is needed. 4. It is expensive, so find out which pumps are covered by your insurance and if those pumps meet your needs. 5. All pumps are an extra piece of hardware attached to your body, either with tubing or attached to your skin. There are many clever ways to wear pumps, and hide them from view, but they do take a bit of getting used to at first. It’s a choice Most people use their pump continuously, but it is not a permanent part of the body. Some kids use it during the school year but not during the summer. Others revert to injections when they go on vacation. Some have issues with their infusion sites, so they go off the pump for a while to let their sites recover. Whatever works to make diabetes treatment easier and better. There are a number of pumps on the market; research what is best for you/your child. Look at the individual pump company sites and read bloggers who have experience using the pumps. Speak with your diabetes team. Most insurance companies will not pay for a new pump more often than every four years, so this is a device you will have for a while. Finally, remember this is not a permanent decision. You can get a pump, wear it, stop wearing it, restart it—whatever works for you. It is an option for treating your diabetes and the choice is yours.

fetched_contents.text: Utility of different glycemic control metrics for optimizing management of diabetes Abstract The benchmark for assessing quality of long-term glycemic control and adjustment of therapy is currently glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c). Despite its importance as an indicator for the development of diabetic complications, recent studies have revealed that this metric has some limitations; it conveys a rather complex message, which has to be taken into consideration for diabetes screening and treatment. On the basis of recent clinical trials, the relationship between HbA1c and cardiovascular outcomes in long-standing diabetes has been called into question. It becomes obvious that other surrogate and biomarkers are needed to better predict cardiovascular diabetes complications and assess efficiency of therapy. Glycated albumin, fructosamin, and 1,5-anhydroglucitol have received growing interest as alternative markers of glycemic control. In addition to measures of hyperglycemia, advanced glucose monitoring methods became available. An indispensible adjunct to HbA1c in routine diabetes care is self-monitoring of blood glucose. This monitoring method is now widely used, as it provides immediate feedback to patients on short-term changes, involving fasting, preprandial, and postprandial glucose levels. Beyond the traditional metrics, glycemic variability has been identified as a predictor of hypoglycemia, and it might also be implicated in the pathogenesis of vascular diabetes complications. Assessment of glycemic variability is thus important, but exact quantification requires frequently sampled glucose measurements. Clinical rationale for considering insulin pump therapy

Insulin pump therapy is being considered because it can offer a more flexible and potentially more precise way to manage Type 1 Diabetes compared with multiple daily injections (MDI). The evidence base supports pump therapy as a tool that may improve glycemic control, especially when used by motivated individuals and when accompanied by appropriate education and follow-up [N3-F3]. The American Diabetes Association (ADA) emphasizes that insulin pumps are a powerful tool when prescribed to appropriate and motivated individuals and can help people achieve their best possible level of glycemic control [N3-F3]. In addition, a meta-analysis of pump therapy in Type 1 Diabetes patients has demonstrated benefits in lowering A1C and reducing hypoglycemia [N3-F3], which is relevant to Mark Walters’ current situation.

One of the main reasons pump therapy may improve glycemic control is that it can reduce the burden of frequent injections and allow more consistent basal insulin delivery. Insulin pumps can help people with diabetes conveniently manage their blood sugar by delivering doses of insulin at programmed rates [N3-R2]. This can be especially helpful for patients who experience variability from injection-related factors, such as inconsistent absorption or difficulty timing boluses around meals [N3-F3]. The ADA notes that pumps do not take away the need to check blood glucose and give insulin before meals, but they can simplify daily management by reducing the number of subcutaneous injections [N2-F2]. In Mark’s case, his current regimen involves Lantus 10 units daily in the morning and Novolog 6 units with meals, and the logs show a wide range of glycemic values from 60 to 280 mg/dL [N1-F1]. A pump may help address some of this variability by providing more continuous basal support and easier bolus adjustments, which can be particularly useful for managing meals and correcting high or low blood glucose more promptly [N3-F3].

In addition to glycemic control, pump therapy may help reduce hypoglycemia risk in some patients. The evidence cited in the ADA resource shows that pumps can reduce hypoglycemia in Type 1 Diabetes patients [N3-F3]. The broader evidence from diabetes technology also suggests that pumps can help improve daily management and reduce the complexity of dose adjustments compared with MDI [N2-F2]. The same source highlights that pumps are not a lifelong commitment, and that the decision to use a pump is a personal one, with the important caveat that pump use requires commitment to blood glucose monitoring and readiness to respond if the pump fails or the infusion set malfunctions [N2-F2]. For Mark, this means that pump therapy could support better daily management while still requiring diligence in blood glucose checks and backup insulin availability.

Overall, the clinical rationale is that pump therapy may improve glycemic control, reduce injection-related variability, and support better daily management and hypoglycemia risk mitigation, provided the patient is motivated, has access to education, and is prepared for the technical and safety responsibilities of pump use [N2-F2][N3-F3].

Clinical evidence and caveats to support the referral

The evidence supporting pump candidacy in adult Type 1 Diabetes is reasonably strong for many patients, but not universal. The ADA notes that insulin pumps have been used successfully across the age spectrum and that whether or not to use a pump is a personal decision; patients can manage diabetes equally well with pumps or multiple injections, so the choice ultimately depends on preference [N2-F2]. The broader diabetes technology evidence also supports pump therapy as a powerful tool when prescribed to appropriate and motivated individuals, with the caveat that it requires education and follow-up [N3-F3]. A meta-analysis has demonstrated benefit in lowering A1C and reducing hypoglycemia in Type 1 Diabetes patients [N3-F3], and the ADA’s 2023 recommendations are summarized in the cited chapter [N3-F3]. However, the evidence is not equally strong for every patient; the ADA also emphasizes that pump use is not a one-size-fits-all solution and that readiness and willingness are critical requirements [N2-F2].

For adult Type 1 Diabetes, the evidence for pump candidacy is strongest when patients are motivated, can manage the technical aspects of pump use, and can commit to frequent blood glucose monitoring [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The evidence also supports pump therapy as an option for people who benefit from changes in basal rates or suspension during exercise, those with frequent hypoglycemia, and those with delayed gastric emptying [N2-F2]. The ADA also notes that pumps do not replace the need for blood glucose checks and bolus insulin before meals, and that the device has limitations such as being only short-acting and requiring backup insulin if it breaks or falls off [N2-F2]. These are important caveats because they mean pump therapy is not automatically the best option for everyone, and it still requires ongoing vigilance.

Important contraindications and barriers include situations where pump use would increase risk or complicate management. The ADA’s contraindications section highlights that pump use is not recommended for patients with impaired level of consciousness, except during short-term anesthesia [N2-R1]. While that is a more hospital-specific concern, it reflects the broader safety principle that pump use requires readiness and safety awareness. In the context of routine care, the main barriers are readiness and willingness, the need for frequent blood glucose checks, the technical complexity of pump operation, and the cost or coverage issue [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that all pumps are an extra piece of hardware attached to the body and that they can be expensive, with insurance coverage typically limited to every four years or so [N2-F2]. These are practical barriers rather than absolute medical contraindications, but they can affect whether a patient is able or willing to pursue pump therapy.

Before pump initiation, typical preparation includes education, training, and readiness assessment. The evidence suggests that patients should be ready and willing to do what it takes to use the pump safely, and most diabetes providers and insurance companies require frequent blood glucose checking before starting a pump [N2-F2]. The same source also notes that pump initiation is not a permanent commitment and that patients may go on and off pumps depending on their needs and challenges [N2-F2]. The broader pump therapy literature also emphasizes that patients need training from a certified pump trainer and that education and follow-up forms are part of the initiation process [N1-F1]. Therefore, the usual preparation is not just a single referral but a sequence of education, readiness assessment, and preparation for pump start-up and ongoing management [N1-F1][N2-F2].

In short, the evidence supports pump candidacy in adult Type 1 Diabetes, especially for motivated patients with variable glycemic control or injection-related challenges, but it also requires readiness, frequent glucose monitoring, and preparation. The caveats include practical barriers such as cost, technical complexity, and the need for backup insulin, as well as safety concerns that make pump therapy unsuitable for some patients [N2-F2][N3-F3].

The evidence supporting pump candidacy in adult Type 1 Diabetes is reasonably strong for many patients, but not universal. For adult Type 1 Diabetes, the evidence for pump candidacy is strongest when patients are motivated, can manage the technical aspects of pump use, and can commit to frequent blood glucose monitoring [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The evidence also supports pump therapy as an option for people who benefit from changes in basal rates or suspension during exercise, those with frequent hypoglycemia, and those with delayed gastric emptying [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that all pumps are an extra piece of hardware attached to the body and that they can be expensive, with insurance coverage typically limited to every four years or so [N2-F2].
